However, despite the impressive advances achieved in static image decoding, the reconstruction of videos from fMRI signals remains challenging due to the temporal mismatch between rapidly changing video stimuli and the slow dynamics of the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) response. We evaluate a Bayesian-inspired proposal-and-rerank strategy on CC2017 and the BOLD Moments Dataset (BMD), using a linear semantic decoder, a pretrained video generator, and three neural encoding streams with ridge readouts and learned pooling in two streams. We refer to this framework as REEL (Reranking Encoder Embeddings with Linear decoding). Compared with a single generated candidate, reranking increases mean Video 50-way accuracy from 0.2359 to 0.2434 across three CC2017 participants and from 0.3653 to 0.3920 across ten BMD participants. These findings suggest an alternative and conceptually simpler strategy for improving video brain decoding, highlighting the potential of our approach as a complementary direction to increasingly complex pipelines.
  </details>

- **[Temporal Pseudo-RGB Encoding for Label-Free Detection of VEEV Infection in Human Brain Endothelial Cells](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21892)**  `arXiv:2611.21892`  
  _Zhengjie Zhu, Stephanie Valdez Trefry, Hao Lu, Abbas Alili, Yongxin Guo, Aarthi Narayanan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Label-free detection of viral infection is central to antiviral screening and pathogen surveillance. Most deep-learning methods analyze individual frames and do not model temporal progression. We evaluate temporal pseudo-RGB encoding, which stacks three time-offset brightfield frames ($t{-}6$ h, $t{-}3$ h, $t$) as the red, green, and blue channels of a single image so that morphological change becomes color and an ImageNet-pretrained convolutional neural network (CNN) can be trained on infection trajectories without architectural modification. In human brain microvascular endothelial cells (HBMVEC) infected with Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV) TC-83, a multi-task network predicts infected-versus-mock status and time post-infection in one forward pass. Across three experimental runs under leave-one-row-out cross-validation, with all 36 wells scored out of fold, the encoding reaches 91.6% accuracy against 87.4% for the single-frame model (paired difference $+4.2$ percentage points, 95% CI $[+2.5, +6.1]$; sign-flip $p = 3\times10^{-5}$; well-level inference, conditional on three runs). At the late-phase endpoint (40-48 h), where floating cells and debris can make conventional brightfield images difficult to interpret, the advantage widens to $+23.9$ points (95% CI $[+19.2, +28.9]$). Time post-infection is recovered on the fixed row split with MAE = 1.31 h ($R^2 = 0.975$). Among the temporal models tested the encoding has the highest mean accuracy, at a fraction of the cost of the recurrent and 3D convolutional alternatives, though only its margin over the single-frame model is resolved; the tested ViT-B/16 backbone showed no corresponding gain, so the finding is limited to convolutional backbones and this virus-cell system.
  </details>

- **[Can a World Model Predict a Deepfake Video? A Consistency Margin Prior for Deepfake Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21846)**  `arXiv:2611.21846`  
  _Pradip Gupta, Shubham Mandloi, Ravi Kumar Satzoda, Sujeeth Bharadwaj, Yassine Benajiba, Dan Roth_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Deepfake detectors often perform well on the dataset they are trained on, but their performance drops when tested on videos from different datasets. In this paper, we study whether a predictive video model can provide a signal that generalizes better across datasets. Instead of relying only on generator-specific artifacts, as many existing detectors do, we use a model trained to predict natural video and measure the difference between what it predicts and what it observes in a video. Using V-JEPA 2.1, we keep the encoder frozen and adapt the predictor using rank-16 LoRA. We define the difference between the predictor output and the frozen encoder target as the prediction residual. We hypothesize that manipulated clips produce, on average, larger prediction residuals than authentic clips, and use this as our consistency-margin prior. We process these residuals using a lightweight Latent Consistency Head (LCH), which separates residual magnitude from direction for training and classification. To test whether the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset generalization, we compare standard and reversed margin objectives while keeping the remaining training setup fixed. We match the two settings on FF++ validation performance before evaluating them on unseen data. The reversed-margin setting exhibits a larger cross dataset generalization gap on average, providing evidence that the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset transfer. Our complete model adds only 8.25M trainable parameters, which is 2.47% of the total 334M parameters. Trained only on FF++, it achieves an AUC of 90.5 on Celeb-DFv2 and performs well across several other cross-dataset benchmarks. Our ablations show that separating residual magnitude from direction, reducing dataset-specific variation, and using a low-rank projection improve cross-dataset generalization in our experiments.
  </details>

- **[Rethinking Perceptual Similarity for Remote Sensing: Multi-Layer Attention Scoring and Human Preference Benchmarking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21816)**  `arXiv:2611.21816`  
  _Eli Underwood, Marc Bosch, Neil Joshi, Jeffrey Wen, Myron Brown_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Perceptual similarity metrics for natural images transfer poorly to remote sensing (RS), where severe geospatial and semantic failures can remain visually plausible while still being decisively wrong for downstream use. To address this, we develop a novel human-aligned perceptual quality metric for generated RS imagery and evaluate it across several generation tasks. We first conduct a controlled perturbation study where we progressively increase the severity of common synthetic perturbations. Using the layer-wise Aligned Attention Score (AAS) responses in RemoteCLIP, we find that different RS artifacts are best captured at different depths. Based on these findings, we introduce Remote Sensing Perceptual Distance (RSPD), a pairwise metric that averages seven independently calibrated layer distances without tuning on human-preference labels. To evaluate our metric on realistic RS generation tasks, we construct a blind, reference-conditioned two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) benchmark with five 300-triplet subsets spanning synthetic artifacts, airborne and spaceborne super-resolution, SAR-to-optical translation, and timeseries controls. We also construct a 300-triplet ordered misregistration benchmark with deterministic labels. Using the same RemoteCLIP checkpoint, RSPD substantially outperforms simple cosine distance with the final global embedding and is competitive with the strongest generic baselines across the realistic RS generation tasks.
  </details>

- **[Sketch, Don't Paint: Allocating Test-Time Compute in Generative Visual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21812)**  `arXiv:2611.21812`  
  _Sheng Lu, Guangpin Tao, Tong Lu, Ying Tai_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multimodal models increasingly reason by synthesizing pixels, sketching maze paths within interleaved chains of thought or rolling out video solutions frame by frame. Each visual thought runs the full diffusion schedule inherited from photorealistic synthesis, so iterative denoising dominates inference cost. We study how to allocate test-time compute along two axes: when to render visual thoughts rather than thinking in text or answering directly, and how many denoising steps each thought requires. Controlled interventions that vary only how the thought is rendered uncover three regimes. Causal thoughts carry the plan and become legible early: an 8-step sketch nearly matches a 50-step render in accuracy, commits to the same plan as often as two independent full renders agree, and in video models mostly fails by stalling short of the goal, so the rollout abstains. Decorative thoughts can be omitted without loss, whereas harmful thoughts lower accuracy. Because the regime depends on both model and task, always drawing is suboptimal. Across 14 model-benchmark pairs of three interleaved reasoners, answering directly, without any thinking, wins 9 pairs, and choosing among direct, text-only, and visual tiers from ten labeled examples per pair raises mean accuracy from 60.7% (always drawing) to 65.1%. Where drawing pays, we propose sketch-and-vote, which samples 8-step sketches (a step count chosen without labels) from independent noises until one answer reaches three votes. With this one setting, sketch-and-vote beats full rendering with fewer denoising steps on an image reasoner and two video reasoners, by 8.6 points on VSP spatial planning and by 9.6 and 22.1 points on mazes.
  </details>

- **[Data-Driven Variable-Length Compression of 3D Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21802)**  `arXiv:2611.21802`  
  _Yvette Y. Lin, Sai Karthikey Pentapati, Sarvesh Sundaram, Guandao Yang, Sara Fridovich-Keil_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Compressing 3D shapes is important for the efficiency of many applications, yet existing methods either cannot leverage dataset-level statistics or use a fixed compression ratio for all shapes. We propose a learned variable-length compression method that exploits structure across a training dataset while adapting compressed representation size to individual shape complexity using only fast feed-forward inference. Our method operates on general latent representations and improves rate-distortion for both meshes and signed distance fields. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Every Camera Grows Up: Camera-Height Regression in Interactive Video World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21782)**  `arXiv:2611.21782`  
  _Sheng Lu, Guangpin Tao, Tong Lu, Ying Tai_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Interactive video world models serve as simulators for embodied agents: from a starting image and an action trajectory, they generate the views the agent would see. The starting image fixes how high the camera is, for example 0.15 m for a floor robot or 2.2 m for an overhead camera, and a faithful simulator must keep this height as the camera moves. We show that six recent open-weight models fail to do so: as motion replaces the starting view with generated content, they move the camera toward human eye level, a failure we call camera-height regression. Our benchmark, EyeHeight, pairs six rendered elevations (0.15 m to 2.2 m) and four calibrated real-world rig heights with scale-free multi-view height estimation. All six models lose their initial height during a $180^\circ$ turn-and-walk rollout: initialized at 0.15 m, only 0-20% of clips end within $1.3\times$ of the starting height as inferred viewpoints converge to human heights of 1.1 m to 1.5 m, whereas ground-truth renders remain within a few percent. In Matrix-Game models, homography-tracked floor motion stays consistent with constant elevation during rotation even as newly outpainted room geometry yields a higher reconstructed viewpoint. Regression grows with rotation angle, begins while the start frame remains in context, and largely reverses in SANA-WM when a $360^\circ$ turn restores the initial view. We trace this pull to human-centric video priors in which floor-level views are nearly absent: in SANA-WM, textual height cues and dense floor-disparity maps do not prevent it, whereas classifier-free text guidance during the first half of denoising strengthens it. Combining unguided sampling with height-balanced fine-tuning recovers more retention but costs 5 MUSIQ points, a loss fixed during those same early steps. Viewpoint drift alone shifts the paths predicted by visual navigation policies.
  </details>

- **[Video recordings and play behaviour annotations of group-housed dairy calves on two Dutch farms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21706)**  `arXiv:2611.21706`  
  _Haiyu Yang, Heidi Lesscher, Enhong Liu, Miel Hostens_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Play is used as an indicator of positive welfare in dairy calves, but openly available video of group-housed calves with individual behaviour annotations is scarce. We describe video from four camera deployments of about one week each in group pens of dairy calves on two farms in the Netherlands: a research and teaching dairy farm (2024 and 2025) and a commercial dairy farm (2024). The recordings comprise 1,173 video files spanning 651 h. For eight observation days, trained observers coded calf behaviour continuously in Noldus The Observer XT with an 18-item ethogram of play and other behaviours, covering 104 h of video, 90 h of which have every calf in the pen coded. The release also contains 1.1 million decoded frames from seven annotated sessions, a per-frame timestamp read by optical character recognition from the camera clock burned into each frame, per-calf segmentation tracks and per-calf frame-level play labels. The data support studies of calf behaviour and welfare and the development and evaluation of automated behaviour recognition.
  </details>

- **[EgoLink: Egocentric Language-Vision Interactive Network Knowledge Challenge Summary](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21690)**  `arXiv:2611.21690`  
  _Renhe Sun, Yueying Feng, Bohan Yu, Tong Niu, Yunqi Liu, Zitong Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The EgoLink Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2026 benchmarks egocentric multimodal intelligence linking first-person perception, social reasoning, and interactive action. Unlike benchmarks centered on visible objects and activities, EgoLink evaluates whether models can interpret emotional and social cues, resolve visually grounded references, and convert user requests into verified tool-mediated actions. Its two tracks cover social reasoning in egocentric video and interactive agents that complete service tasks through dialogue, tool use, and closed-loop execution. Together, they test whether perception, reasoning, and decision-making remain coupled under both offline question answering and state-changing interaction. We highlight a multi-stage Track 1 data pipeline for multiple-choice question (MCQ) generation, chain-of-thought generation, automatic quality grading, and video-contribution filtering. We summarize the task design, evaluation metrics, rules, leaderboards, and representative solutions. The benchmark combines objective answer scoring with process- and result-based evaluation, enabling analysis of both final correctness and execution quality. The best Track 1 system achieved 0.9263 accuracy, while the best Track 2 system achieved 0.844 joint success and 0.916 micro accuracy. Participant reports reveal a shared principle: strong systems make intermediate evidence explicit through candidate verification, option-robust reasoning, scenario-aware planning, tool canonicalization, and state-aware correction before answering or acting. These findings highlight the importance of process verification and evidence-grounded reasoning for reliable egocentric multimodal intelligence.
  </details>

- **[Edge-Adaptive Hiera-Seg Model for Building-Integrated Photovoltaic Power Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21680)**  `arXiv:2611.21680`  
  _Na Yu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Building integrated photovoltaic power forecasting is challenging because facade orientation, rooftop geometry, nearby buildings, vegetation, cloud movement, module temperature, inverter status and edge device reliability jointly affect power generation. This paper proposes an edge-adaptive HieraSeg model for short term BIPV power forecasting with multi-orientation visual-irradiance fusion. RGB facade images, optional thermal cues, irradiance measurements, module temperature, facade orientation, rooftop masks, shading labels, sky condition, historical power and edge device state are aligned into synchronous forecasting windows. HieraSeg extracts hierarchical regions from facade, rooftop, sky, shadow and background images, while the edge-adaptive module changes feature weights under missing frames, latency shifts and local shading changes. The segmentation branch identifies occluded module areas and separates facade, rooftop, sky and background evidence before the forecasting head estimates future BIPV output. Experiments are designed on a simulated multibuilding BIPV dataset with unseen building and unseen orientation tests. The model reports predicted power, confidence interval, dominant evidence, occlusion contribution, orientation contribution and energy-management review priority. This output is intended to show whether the forecast is driven by irradiance change, visible shading, orientation response, stale edge information or recent power history. The framework supports local forecasting at edge controllers with limited communication delay and computing resources, linking visual occlusion, irradiance dynamics and power history to traceable forecasting results for building energy management, microgrid scheduling and BIPV operation planning.
  </details>

- **[Depth-Aware Activation Steering via Attention Residuals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21655)**  `arXiv:2611.21655`  
  _Shilong Zhao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Activation steering is a simple, training-free way to modulate LLM behavior, yet existing methods typically inject vectors at a single layer and lack mechanisms for depth-aware propagation or internal verification. We combine two recent ideas - Attention Residuals (AttnRes) providing learnable cross-layer pathways, and Jacobian-lens (J-space) concept readout - into a lightweight depth-aware steering pipeline. On two small open models (Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3.5-0.8B), distributing a persona vector according to AttnRes-style depth weights yields stronger internal alignment (deeper-layer concept cosine and rank, p<0.0001) and stronger behavioral shifts than single-layer injection. The effect is sign-specific: reverse vectors invert all six metrics, random directions degrade alignment (p<0.0001), and a short LoRA fine-tune erases the imprint. Injection rewires attention strictly downstream of the injection point (upstream JS = 0.00000). Three practical findings follow. First, a layer-wise geometric decomposition of cosine readouts: at the injection layer 123% of the increase is arithmetic, while 5-11 layers downstream 100% is dynamical. Second, an intensity window: effects are monotone over 0.3-0.7, then generation collapses (617 to 306 to 25 chars). Third, metric discipline: keyword-rule metrics fail LLM-judge validation (kappa <= 0.09), and two rule-based conclusions were retracted. Training the depth weights on a steering objective (200 steps, frozen backbone) raises final alignment 10x on held-out prompts. Cross-persona vectors retain 96-99% of the effect: specificity holds against random, not semantic, directions. We contribute a practical, low-overhead depth-aware steering method with a careful evaluation protocol. Code and data are released.
  </details>

- **[DuoFlow: Towards Synchronized Speech and Motion Generation with Fine-Grained Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21530)**  `arXiv:2611.21530`  
  _Jun Dong, Ronghui Li, Zhongyuan Hu, Yunqi Zhao, Lijie Guo, Ruizhang Xu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  An embodied speaker's expressiveness depends not only on what is said, but also on how the voice sounds and how the body moves. However, existing joint speech-motion generation models are largely driven implicitly by transcript semantics or intermediate speech representations, offering little explicit control over motion hierarchy, body parts, or vocal style. To bridge this gap, we construct MotionSpeech, a structured benchmark for controllable joint speech-motion generation that includes transcripts, voice-style descriptions, and motion conditions at two hierarchical levels. Building on this benchmark, we propose DuoFlow, a dual-stream latent flow transformer that jointly denoises speech and motion under a shared noise level and a unified second-based temporal coordinate. Modality-specific residual connectors inject structured conditions into the corresponding streams, layer-wise bidirectional cross-modal attention coordinates their generation, and a monotonic phoneme pathway combines normalized progress anchors with CTC supervision to strengthen speech temporal modeling. DuoFlow provides a unified interface for fine-grained motion and vocal-style control and demonstrates the ability to synthesize high-quality, synchronized, and instruction-consistent speech-motion sequences. Project page,this https URL.
  </details>

- **[LynnReal-Hand: Unlocking World Interaction with Hand Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21479)**  `arXiv:2611.21479`  
  _Shaohao Rui, Chaoyang Zhang, Xiaofeng Mao, Weijie Ma_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.
  </details>

- **[A Study on Performance Enhancement of a Webcam-Based Real-Time Eye-Tracking System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21233)**  `arXiv:2611.21233`  
  _Minuk Jung, Kyeonghun Kim, Sooyeon Yoon_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This study proposes a real-time gaze-tracking system that uses a standard RGB webcam to estimate screen coordinates. The system combines ETH-XGaze-based gaze estimation with nine-point calibration and polynomial ridge regression. To reduce errors caused by changes in head position, it also applies a conditional residual correction derived from head and pose features extracted with RTMPose. Whether this correction is used depends on the reliability of the detected features and the characteristics of the calibration data. In a preliminary experiment, one participant completed trials at 12 screen targets. The resulting mean screen-coordinate error was 204.24 pixels, which was 35.83% lower than that of xgaze-js and 57.69% lower than that of gaze_tracker. The system produced valid gaze estimates for all 12 targets. These preliminary findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining user-specific calibration with conditional pose-based correction for webcam gaze tracking. Because the evaluation involved only one participant, further experiments with more participants and a wider range of postures are required.
  </details>

- **[IGRecon4D: Dynamic-Object-Aware Feed-Forward Reconstruction of Driving Scenes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21126)**  `arXiv:2611.21126`  
  _Yifei Tong, Ziyang Huang, Yizhao Han, Xiaoxiao Long, Hao Zhu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Feed-forward 4D driving-scene reconstruction enables efficient modeling of dynamic autonomous-driving scenes, but current methods suffer from two complementary failure modes: semantic leakage of traffic participants into the static representation and geometric drift of Gaussian locations across viewpoints. We propose \textbf{IGRecon4D}, a feed-forward dynamic scene reconstruction framework that addresses these failures with training-time instance-prior distillation and LiDAR-anchored Gaussian positioning. Specifically, an instance-level semantic branch provides a potentially dynamic participant prior, which is distilled into dynamic-mask learning through the Instance-Dynamic Consistency Constraint to encourage high-recall localization of traffic-participant regions prone to dynamic-static leakage. In parallel, sparse LiDAR measurements guide dense depth estimation, and the resulting depths are back-projected to anchor Gaussian positions for improved multi-view geometric consistency. Experiments on the Waymo Open Dataset and zero-shot evaluation on nuScenes demonstrate improved full-image reconstruction on the main benchmark and stronger traffic-participant-region reconstruction under cross-dataset evaluation.
  </details>

- **[Dataset Distillation for Handwritten Text Recognition: An Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21054)**  `arXiv:2611.21054`  
  _Félix Fuentes-Hurtado, Aric Ayllón, Juan C. Alfaro_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Dataset distillation (DD) replaces large training datasets with smaller synthetic ones to reduce computational costs. While traditionally used for classification, we present, to our knowledge, the first DD study for line-level handwritten text recognition (HTR). Unlike classification tasks, which use discrete labels, HTR employs unaligned sequences from a virtually infinite output space as labels. To adapt classification-based DD methods to this scenario, we define text pseudo-classes by clustering transcriptions based on character n-grams. We adapt gradient matching (GM), distribution matching (DM) and trajectory matching (MTT) to a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN) trained with Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC). In this process, synthetic line images are generated by optimising only the pixels of real starting lines (either randomly chosen or selected as text medoids), while keeping their original transcriptions fixed. Across four datasets (IAM, George Washington, READ\,2016, LAM) and three budgets (1--10\,\% of the training lines), no distilled set outperforms its real initialisation lines. Random lines prove better than medoids, and further optimisation only degrades recognition. Methodologically, DM lowers its objective without benefit, while GM and MTT barely move theirs. We turn these findings into guidelines for evaluating data compression in HTR.
  </details>

- **[ScoutCache: Efficient Few-Step Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Conditional Readout and Selective Caching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21038)**  `arXiv:2611.21038`  
  _Hao Tan, Jinghui Qin, Xuming Hu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables efficient long video generation, but inference still incurs substantial computational costs from repeated denoising and KV cache operations. Existing acceleration methods reduce parts of this overhead, while historical KV reading and cache construction remain costly across video chunks. To address these challenges, we propose ScoutCache, a training-free framework that jointly optimizes denoising, historical KV reading, and cache construction. We observe that shallow feature changes provide useful information for estimating clean latent updates, while historical KV dependence varies across Transformer layers and attention heads but remains relatively stable across video chunks. Based on these observations, we develop Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations. We further introduce Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical reading budgets based on attention output perturbations, and Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to reduce cache construction costs by selecting informative spatial tokens while maintaining spatial coverage. Extensive experiments on Self-Forcing and LongLive using VBench and MovieGen demonstrate that ScoutCache achieves up to 2.28$\times$ and 1.86$\times$ speedups, respectively, while consistently improving generation quality without modifying pretrained model parameters.
  </details>

- **[FAVR: Flow-Aware Visual Residual Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20971)**  `arXiv:2611.20971`  
  _Qixuan Wu, Xiaole Yang, Yuguang Yang, Canyu Chen, Linlin Yang, Haixia Pan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Pretrained video representations provide rich temporal information for robotic manipulation, yet effectively integrating them into existing vision-language-action (VLA) policies remains challenging. We present Flow-Aware Visual Residual Alignment (FAVR), a lightweight framework for flow-aware visual conditioning of frozen VLA policies. FAVR maintains a compact temporal visual state through linear Test-Time Training (TTT) and retrieves action-conditioned visual features throughout flow-based action generation. By exploiting the affine structure of the frozen action head, we explicitly characterize how injected visual features influence predicted action velocities and formulate flow-aware channel selection as a box-constrained optimization problem. We develop a FISTA-based solver for joint gate optimization and derive an efficient closed-form approximation through diagonalization and rescaling. With only 1.74-2.19M trainable parameters and 5,000 adaptation steps, FAVR improves pretrained VLA policies across benchmarks. On RoboTwin 2.0, FAVR improves LingBot-VLA from 87.12% to 90.04% under clean conditions and from 86.88% to 89.38% under randomized conditions. A controlled ablation on five RoboTwin tasks further shows that flow-aware gating increases average success from 72.0% with a gate shared across flow steps to 82.0%, demonstrating the benefit of adapting visual conditioning throughout action generation.
  </details>

- **[ASCG: Adaptive Spatial Classifier Guidance for Surgical Concept Suppression in Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20625)**  `arXiv:2611.20625`  
  _Younghwan Kil, Joonhyeong Park, Giung Nam, Juho Lee_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  While text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models achieve remarkable quality, they risk producing harmful content. Existing safety mechanisms often rely on indiscriminate, global interventions that induce unintended semantic drift and degrade image quality. To address this, we propose Adaptive Spatial Classifier Guidance (ASCG), a necessity-driven framework that employs probabilistic monitoring to activate guidance selectively upon harm detection. By leveraging Grad-CAM for localized suppression, ASCG effectively removes harmful concepts while preserving superior semantic fidelity compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, we overcome the limitations of traditional metrics like NudeNet---which fails to assess semantic integrity---by introducing a VLM-based evaluation framework to provide a fine-grained, robust analysis of both safety and context preservation. Our results demonstrate that ASCG not only balances safety and fidelity but also exhibits remarkable plug-and-play synergy with existing frameworks to establish state-of-the-art performance.
  </details>

- **[ReScene: Incremental Scene Chronology from Sparse Revisits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20433)**  `arXiv:2611.20433`  
  _Wei Qin Chuah, Zeji Hui, Amirali Khodadadian Gostar, Alireza Bab-Hadiashar_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Scene chronology aims to reconstruct a scene across visits separated by hours or days, during which objects may change in position, presence or shape. Such reconstruction must retain every earlier state, yet each revisit often provides only a few images. Storing a complete model for each visit duplicates the unchanged scene, whereas updating a single shared model alters earlier states. We present ReScene, which stores each visit as an immutable compact update, so that any earlier visit can be recovered exactly by applying the stored updates in order, without retaining past images. To localise each update, ReScene attributes the disagreement between the preceding reconstruction and the new images to individual Gaussians through their compositing weights. This attribution guides the suppression of outdated Gaussians and the refinement of persistent ones, while newly visible surfaces are initialised from learned multi-view depth. We also introduce Multi-State, a benchmark of non-rigid deformation and partial material removal, including synthetic scenes with ground-truth geometry. ReScene achieves quality higher than sequential 3DGS checkpointing with 2.5--4.8$\times$ less uncompressed history storage. At comparable PSNR, it also reduces foreground depth error by 3.2$\times$ relative to sequential ChronoGS, showing that accurate rendering does not necessarily imply accurate geometry. Code and benchmark are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20385)**  `arXiv:2611.20385`  
  _Emilio Ferrara_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 75% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 40%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 80-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.
  </details>

- **[Latent World Modeling for Point-Cloud Video Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20090)**  `arXiv:2611.20090`  
  _Zhuoyue Zhang, Jian Liu, Jihua Zhu, Ajmal Saeed Mian_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Masked modeling is the dominant self-supervised paradigm for point-cloud videos. However, it leaks the information it is meant to predict, whether it reconstructs masked points as in MAE-style methods or predicts their latent features. Because point-cloud tokens are anchored at points sampled from each frame, querying a target at its own position reveals where its geometry has moved, in reconstruction and latent prediction alike. For latent predictors, random spatio-temporal masks introduce a further shortcut, as visible frames on both sides of each target allow interpolation rather than forecasting. The pretext task thus reduces to completion. Once the target positions are withheld, a masked latent predictor performs only slightly better than copying the last frame. To remove this leakage, we propose PointWM, a latent world model that turns completion into forecasting by predicting the features and geometry of future frames from strictly earlier context. Each target is queried only with its last-seen position and timestamp, while a latent action learned without annotations is meant to capture the part of the future that the past leaves undetermined. On HOI4D action segmentation with a P4Transformer backbone, PointWM improves F1@50 over training from scratch by 24.9 offline and 29.1 under strictly causal inference. These results show the promise of latent world models as a leakage-free pretraining paradigm for point-cloudthis http URLcode is publicly available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[What Matters for Cross-Modal Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20000)**  `arXiv:2611.20000`  
  _Yipeng Sun, Jiajun Wang, Siyuan Mei, Yan Xia, Siming Bayer, Vincent Christlein, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that models trained on different modalities converge toward a shared representation. Related work aligns frozen image and text encoders on natural images without paired data. We test zero-pair alignment on five datasets across four modalities: natural images, environmental audio, chest radiographs, and 3D computed tomography (CT). It succeeds only on COCO and fails on the other four. We analyze the failures and find that alignment must first locate the subspace where the modalities co-vary and then orient the mapping within it. Consistent with previous studies, medical imaging is the hardest case: its shared subspace carries the smallest fraction of the variance. When this fraction is small, alignment needs image-text pairs, and random-matrix theory predicts how many pairs are needed. These findings motivate LightAlign: a few pairs let a ridge regression between two frozen encoders locate and orient the mapping simultaneously, and a classifier fitted only on report text then predicts findings from the mapped images. On 3D CT, LightAlign surpasses models trained end to end on image-report pairs without finding-level labels: with only 200 pairs, LightAlign outperforms CT-CLIP on CT-RATE (0.754 vs. 0.733 AUROC), and with only 100 CT-RATE pairs, it does so on RAD-ChestCT, an out-of-distribution dataset from a different hospital. On CheXpert, it reaches 0.862 mean AUROC with only about 5% as many pairs as models trained on MIMIC-CXR.
  </details>

- **[A Threshold-Free Visual-Semantic Matching Metric for Evaluating Consistency in Subject-Driven Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19780)**  `arXiv:2611.19780`  
  _Bowei Shan, Heng Yin_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We propose a Threshold-Free Visual-Sematic Matching (TF-VSM) metric, to quantitatively evaluate localized visual consistency across varying poses and environments in subject-driven text-to-image generation. TF-VSM is a fully continuous, threshold-free visual consistency metric paired with an extended feature-disentanglement retraining schedule for dual-branch ResNet feature-aggregation networks. Existing metrics suffer from point-alignment dropouts, threshold sensitivity, and score instability. To address them, our TF-VSM, rather than enforcing rigid binary cutoffs ($T_s$, $T_v$), weights every object point by a non-linear semantic match confidence $w_j = ReLU(\hat s_j)^2$ to yield a closed-form confidence-weighted score without any hand-tuned hyperparameters. Experimental results show that, TF-VSM attains Pearson 0.638 and Spearman 0.674 oracle correlation, improving over the pretrained VSM baseline (0.454/0.589) by +0.171/ + 0.116 after retraining, and drastically outperforming CLIP (-0.052/ -0.004), DINO (0.087/0.121), and VLMs (0.096/0.003). Six diagnostic ablations confirm that smooth confidence weighting is the right mechanism, that hard semantic gating is brittle (dropping to 0.533 Pearson at $T_s$=0.8), and that the threshold-free metric is essentially invariant to the training time loss balance $\alpha$. Code is available at:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[TIVS: Mapping the Sensitivity Landscape of Visual Token Transformations in MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19745)**  `arXiv:2611.19745`  
  _Yikang Qiao, Jianye Zeng, Duan Huang, Ziying Song_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent efforts to improve the efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have explored visual token pruning, quantization, and feature compression. However, the properties that determine whether transformed visual tokens remain usable by a frozen decoder are not well characterized. We introduce \textbf{TIVS (Token Identity Versus Statistics)}, a training-free intervention framework that separately studies sequence permutation, token retention, numerical precision, and statistical replacement under controlled conditions. On 192 POPE questions, three token permutations change TinyLLaVA accuracy by only $-0.17$ percentage points on average, while changing 4.69\% of individual predictions. Diagonal and rank-64 Gaussian replacements decrease accuracy by 25.0 and 28.1 points on the same subset. Further experiments with exact moment constraints, quantization error, token retention, and additional visual tasks reveal how strongly the effects depend on the original feature values and the evaluation setting. These findings provide an empirical basis for assessing visual token transformations in frozen MLLMs and designing more reliable multimodal interfaces.
  </details>

- **[Guided Group Featurizers (GGF): Improving Block-Sparse Featurizers with Object-Guided Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18861)**  `arXiv:2611.18861`  
  _Waldemar Chang, Andrii Krutsylo_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Block-sparse featurizers (BSFs) use groups of learned directions to capture the multidimensional structure of visual concepts. However, grouping alone does not ensure that information about a concept is consolidated within a single group. We introduce Guided Group Featurizers (GGF), a novel object-guided extension that uses object annotations for initialization and training while preserving the BSF architecture. We assess whether each group's strongest response regions share an object type, part or material across images. Blinded GPT reviews give GGF groups an average semantic coherence score of $93.4\pm1.6$%, versus $83.4\pm2.5$% for SLiCS and $67.9\pm3.1$% for supervised Vanilla BSF. GGF also leads in a separate blinded Gemini review. GGF's consolidation advantage extends to unguided categories: one selected group per category covers $66.1\pm1.9$% of target-containing crops, versus $59.2\pm1.8$% for supervised Vanilla BSF, at approximately 5% false-positive rates for both. Across COCO and VOC, GGF also improves single-group object Capture and localization over Vanilla BSFs, SLiCS and Concept-SAE. Its groups produce more focused and reproducible object responses while supporting recognition and retaining associations under rotation, scale and brightness changes. GGF also uses fewer learned parameters than Concept-SAE and shorter recorded VOC training loops than both supervised alternatives. These findings support object guidance for organizing more interpretable BSF groups and show that response concentration extends to categories excluded from guidance.
  </details>

- **[LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6 Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18822)**  `arXiv:2611.18822`  
  _Meituan LongCat Team, Xunliang Cai, Yiqi Chen, Feng Gao, Xiaoyu Kong, Le Li, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent advances in audio-driven avatar video generation have enabled increasingly realistic synthesis, yet achieving precise lip-audio synchronization, natural, human-like motion, and visual consistency over long sequences remains challenging. We present LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6, which builds on LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.5 to improve expressive naturalness and reduce error accumulation during extended generation, e.g., exaggerated lip movements and overly red, temporally unstable lip coloration, enhance the naturalness of facial expressions and coordinated head and body movements. These improvements are driven by a refined post-training pipeline that integrates reinforcement learning, improved classifier-free guidance strategies for DMD-based few-step distillation, long-video rollouts, and on-policy distillation. Together, these refinements improve expressive realism and enable the generation of videos exceeding 10 minutes while maintaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Arena evaluations show that LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6 outperforms its predecessor and competing commercial audio-driven avatar models, demonstrating the effectiveness of the improved post-training pipeline.
  </details>

- **[AerialOcc: Unified 3D Aerial Perception without Task-Specific Head](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18770)**  `arXiv:2611.18770`  
  _Fan Liu, Xiang Gu, Baoyu Lv, Chuanyi Zhang, Liang Yao, Yuye Ma, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Aerial perception systems are increasingly expected to support diverse tasks, yet existing solutions remain fundamentally tied to task-specific outputs. Detection, segmentation, and other perception objectives are usually learned either by separate models or by sharing a backbone with multiple task heads, leaving the model itself unaware of the common structure underlying these tasks. We are interested in asking: can a single perception representation support different levels of understanding without being designed for any specific task? We notice that occupancy is a promising task-agnostic representation for drone perception. By modeling the spatial existence and semantics of the environment, it naturally bridges different perception granularities, from coarse scene understanding to fine-grained object localization. Therefore, we introduce AerialOcc, a unified occupancy-based perception model that enables multiple drone perception tasks from a single inference process, without maintaining task-specific prediction heads. To facilitate this direction, we construct AerialOcc-20K, a large-scale multi-class occupancy dataset for aerial environments. Extensive experiments show that AerialOcc achieves competitive performance across diverse perception tasks while preserving a unified architecture. Our findings demonstrate that occupancy can serve as a universal perception interface, offering a new perspective toward flexible and scalable visual intelligence for autonomous drones from a common 3D scene representation. Models and data are publicly available atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[Pl@ntNet machine-to-machine identification service with Pl@ntNet API: enabling automated biodiversity monitoring through large-scale plant identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16538)**  `arXiv:2611.16538`  
  _Benjamin Bourel, Jean-Christophe Lombardo, Alexis Joly, Mathias Chouet, Thomas Paillot, Antoine Affouard, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  1. Monitoring plant biodiversity requires identifying large numbers of plants across space and time. Although artificial intelligence (AI) can now identify plant species from images with high accuracy, most existing systems rely on users manually submitting images. As ecological monitoring increasingly generates large image collections from cameras, drones, robots and online platforms, there is a growing need for plant identification services that can be directly integrated into automated data-processing workflows.2. Here, we present Pl@ntNet's machine-to-machine AI plant identification service. This service uses an application programming interface (API) to provide programmatic access to Pl@ntNet's plant recognition models and the associated taxonomic processing. This service enables the implementation of automated identification workflows without human intervention and can thus directly link large image collections and automated observation systems to an AI-based plant identification system.3. We establish that this service, which covers 85,000 species from around the world, (1) has a species prediction accuracy of 0.89, (2) process images up to 666 times faster than workflows requiring human intervention, (3) and has processed over 84 million identification requests since its launch, including more than 40 million in 2025 alone. We demonstrate how it has already enabled the implementation of a new generation of ecological workflows. Finally, we illustrate its application using a reproducible example: identifying plants from insect photos on iNaturalist.4. In conclusion, this machine-to-machine species identification is already operating on a considerable scale and meets a genuine need. All of this paves the way for a new paradigm in biodiversity monitoring, in which automated sensors and image collections can be directly connected to AI-based identification services.
  </details>

- **[FuGIBench: Evaluating Reliable Preparation in Streaming Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16400)**  `arXiv:2611.16400`  
  _Changheng Cai, Zhichao Huang, Song Ren, Zhichen Zhao, Hongsen Liu, Chaoyang Zheng, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  An assistant watching a worker can prepare for an emerging need before the worker is ready to receive help. As the need evolves, the assistant must maintain preparation until a response is due, or withdraw it if the need disappears. Video anticipation and interactive response benchmarks leave this interval between early evidence and response largely unmeasured. We introduce FuGIBench (Future-Grounded Interaction), a streaming-video benchmark in which a model chooses among waiting, reversible preparation, and response given a causal video prefix and a task contract. The benchmark contains 19,893 synthetic tool-assistance videos across ten tool tasks, in handover, ordinary-activity, and cancelled-need tracks. One primary score credits sustained preparation, incorporates response-interval alignment, and penalizes activity when the reference prescribes waiting. On a frozen set of 1,000 episodes, a reference system with a longer preparation lead has poorer response alignment, while similar handover leads accompany different levels of activity during ordinary work in matched scenarios. Together with cancellation analyses, these results show why evaluating preparation requires tracking decisions as needs develop, become actionable, or disappear.
  </details>

- **[EmoReward: Self-Evolving Reward Calibration for Emotional Video Generation RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06518)**  `arXiv:2611.06518`  
  _Mingzhe Zheng, Yue Wu, Jing Tan, Chang Zou, Dengyang Jiang, Zeyue Tian, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has advanced generative model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, but evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Existing approaches typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that poorly capture emotional intent and can invite reward hacking, while RLHF is difficult to scale and subject to individual aesthetic differences that complicate the calibration of facial, body motion, and chromatic cues across narrative contexts. We introduce EmoReward, a new self-evolving training mechanism that distills evidence reliability from reward traces collected during an actual training run to adaptively guide multi-reward weight allocation in subsequent training by determining which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. EmoReward first plans specific grounding cues from the emotional prompt to guide evaluation, then uses heterogeneous signal primitives to score the generated video during the act stage. Reflective Reward Gating calibrates their contributions through instance-level gates for phase, face confidence, conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over the active set to produce the sample's fused reward. RewardMemory then estimates each primitive's reliability from rollout scores and outcomes within each emotional regime in the finished training run, then fixes bounded multipliers that calibrate fusion weights in the next training run without updating reward models. Experiments on HunyuanVideo 1.5 show improvements across multiple RL algorithms and compare EmoReward with other agentic reward methods under SAGE-GRPO. Ablations and transfer experiments on SD 3.5 and FLUX further support adaptive reward calibration for visual generation.
  </details>

- **[Recoverability-Aware Evaluation of Diffusion Video Inpainting and Object Removal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01578)**  `arXiv:2611.01578`  
  _Yanliang Qi, Jiacheng Ding, Cong Guo, Peihua Mai_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Video inpainting for object removal is scored over the whole hole, although the background behind the object is visible in other frames of the shot for some hole pixels and in no frame for others. A whole-hole score therefore mixes copying with generation and cannot show which of the two a remover does well. To separate the two, we propose recoverability-stratified evaluation, in which a point tracker run on the clean video labels each hole pixel by whether and how far away it is observed, so that fidelity and temporal stability can be reported per stratum against a copy reference. To reuse the observed content, we also propose evidence-guided sampling (EGS), which blends tracked colors into the clean-latent prediction of a video diffusion remover without training. On DAVIS, the perceptual advantage of three diffusion removers over flow propagation shrinks where the content is visible a few frames away (LPIPS difference-in-differences +0.046 to +0.056 against E2FGVI-HQ), and real paired captures show the same pattern for two of them. Their DAVIS hole warping error is two to four times that of ProPainter, and copying along clean-video tracks lowers their recoverable LPIPS by a quarter to two fifths. EGS closes 43% and 56% of the gap to this copy reference on held-out DAVIS when its colors come from clean-video tracks. With colors tracked on the masked input, a pre-registered confirmation finds no gain on MiniMax-Remover and a loss on ROSE. Diffusion removers thus leave observed content unused on DAVIS, and training-free reuse does not yet hold with tracked evidence.
  </details>

- **[Spend the Bits Where the Tiny Objects Are: Rate-Utility Region Coding for Aerial Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01573)**  `arXiv:2611.01573`  
  _Yanliang Qi, Jiacheng Ding, Cong Guo, Peihua Mai_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Bandwidth-limited aerial cameras must compress their images before a remote detector can find the many tiny objects in them. Threshold-based region-of-interest (ROI) coding sends only confidently detected regions, and because tiny objects provide limited visual evidence and often score low, it can discard the regions that contain them. We propose rate-utility region coding (RUO), which sends a region when its expected detection utility justifies its measured byte cost, choosing to drop it or to send it at low or high quality with one multiplier shared across images. RUO trains no model, uses a standard image codec and decodes in a few milliseconds. On all 1,610 VisDrone-DET test-dev images, RUO uses 42.4% fewer bits than a tuned threshold-based ROI coder, averaged over their shared tiny-object average precision (AP) range. RUO also needs fewer bits for tiny objects than the AV1 Image File Format (AVIF), High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC) and three published learned codecs, and its advantage over threshold-based ROI coding persists when the sender and receiver use different detectors. For AP over all object sizes RUO needs 25.4% more bits than the tuned ROI coder, because its allocation drops large regions first at low rates, so it suits tasks that target tiny objects. We plan to release the code.
  </details>

- **[Grounding Across Views: Cross-View Referring Reasoning for Visual Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01074)**  `arXiv:2611.01074`  
  _Hao Gan, Liuqian Wang, Zhuping Hu, Yufei Gao, Wentao Chao, Chong Fu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) aims to identify a query-view target in a satellite image, yet reliable instance grounding remains challenging under substantial viewpoint discrepancies. Although recent methods incorporate multimodal prompts, they insufficiently address the varying transferability of linguistic and visual evidence across views. Viewpoint-dependent descriptions (e.g., building facades visible in oblique UAV views but not in top-down satellite images) may become unreliable for satellite grounding, while visually similar instances further complicate target identification. To address these challenges, we rethink CVOGL from a visual grounding perspective and propose GAV (Grounding Across Views), a view-aware framework for constructing target-centered evidence and establishing discriminative cross-view correspondence. Specifically, view-aware referring reasoning mitigates viewpoint-dependent ambiguity, multi-token exemplar prompting and contrastive alignment strengthen visual-semantic correspondence, and scene-level supervision with alignment-based verification distinguishes competing satellite instances. We further introduce CVOGL-Text, a street- and drone-to-satellite benchmark with query-derived expressions. GAV achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoP-UAV with 62.55% Acc@0.5 (+18.19 percentage points) and outperforms evaluated click-point baselines on CVOGL-Text.
  </details>

- **[Wizard: Manipulate Any World in Real Time via Agentic Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40339)**  `arXiv:2610.40339`  
  _Yuzhe Wu, Zijun Lin, Cheston Tan, Bihan Wen, Yeying Jin_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent advances in video world models have enabled increasingly realistic and interactive virtual environments, opening new possibilities for player-customizable gameplay. Agentic frameworks further advance this direction by decoupling explicit game logic and controllable world representations from visual generation. However, existing approaches support only simple game settings and predefined motion patterns, generalize poorly to unseen environments and characters, and offer limited real-time interactivity. In this paper, we introduce Wizard, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, precise control over character motions while generalizing zero-shot across novel scenes, characters, and actions. To achieve this, we construct a diverse dataset spanning 805 scenes and 178 characters, incorporating skeleton and geometry information as structured proxies to condition video generation. Our agentic framework explicitly tracks and updates game states to support character-aware adaptive masking and world-anchored spatial conditioning, improving character identity preservation and spatial consistency. Experiments on WBench show that our method achieves higher gameplay fidelity with comparable video quality and spatiotemporal consistency, while using fewer parameters and less training data than state-of-the-art world models. These advantages are also retained in our two-step real-time variant. Overall, Wizard combines agentic control with structured proxy-based generation to enable player-driven game creation with real-time, generalizable, and mechanically consistent world simulation.
  </details>

- **[Automated open-set multi-view seahorse re-identification from underwater photograph sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39857)**  `arXiv:2610.39857`  
  _Tristan Fauvel, Sylvie Louisy, Patrick Louisy, Thomas Fauvel_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Automated animal re-identification from photograph sequences can facilitate minimally invasive Capture-Mark-Recapture studies at scale. Yet, photographs taken during an observation session can vary greatly in quality, not always providing the necessary information for accurate re-identification. In this paper, we present new methods for open-set re-identification from image sequences. We train and evaluate taxonomic classification, sex determination and reidentification models on a dataset of 35,914 photographs of 474 individual seahorses observed in the wild. Combining the photographs of an observation improves all three tasks. For species and sex, a linear probe on DINOv3 embeddings classifies each photograph, and we average the logits over the photographs of an observation. At the observation level, this model reaches a balanced accuracy of 0.97 for species and 0.90 for sex. For open-set re-identification, a fine-tuned MiewID descriptor retrieves candidate individuals, and a learned relevance score weights each photograph. Local feature matching with ALIKED and LightGlue combined with a geometric check with RANSAC that keeps only the consistent matches then reranks the candidates. A logistic model estimates the probability that the individual is already in the gallery. A maximum a posteriori rule then chooses between the best-matching identity and a new individual. This method reaches a normalized accuracy of 0.90 when the gallery holds every past observation of each individual, and 0.83 when it holds only one.
  </details>

- **[SAGE: Saliency-Aware Generalist Encoder with Multi-level Feature Enhancement for Visual Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36719)**  `arXiv:2610.36719`  
  _Junyu Chen, Yucheng Huang, Le Yang, Qi Dang, Xin Kong, Haifeng Huo, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Pretrained vision transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated strong transferability across visual recognition tasks. However, adapting a shared representation to diverse downstream tasks remains challenging, as different tasks demand varying levels of semantic abstraction and spatial precision. We present SAGE (Saliency-Aware Generalist Encoder), an encoder-side architecture that enhances pretrained ViT representations by integrating multi-depth features, register-token context, saliency-guided modulation, and aligned local views into a unified multi-scale feature pyramid. Evaluated with ViT-B and ViT-L backbones on six visual tasks across seven benchmarks, SAGE achieves 62.8 box AP, 55.3 mask AP, and 78.5 keypoint AP on COCO; 60.3 semantic segmentation mIoU and 44.9 instance segmentation AP on ADE20K; 94.76\% classification top-1 accuracy on TinyImageNet; and 81.10 oriented detection AP$_{50}$ on DIOR-R. Combined with a progressive two-stage training strategy, SAGE-L achieves the best performance among the selected reference methods in six of the seven benchmark settings, while remaining competitive on keypoint estimation against substantially larger models. Importantly, these tasks share the same SAGE encoder and multi-scale feature interface, while employing task-specific prediction heads. To the best of our knowledge, SAGE is the first publicly reported encoder to achieve highly competitive results on six visual tasks across seven benchmarks, demonstrating its generality and competitiveness.
  </details>

- **[ARISE: Authentic Reference-Informed Stability Enhancement for Continual Multimodal Forgery Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36509)**  `arXiv:2610.36509`  
  _Yuchen Zhang, Yaxiong Wang, Yujiao Wu, Lianwei Wu, Qi Zhang, Li Zhu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multimodal forgery detection is commonly studied under a static assumption: training attacks are expected to approximate those encountered after deployment. This assumption becomes increasingly fragile as generators, editing systems, and multimodal large language models continually introduce new forgery mechanisms and forensic evidence. We formulate this problem as attack-incremental continual multimodal forgery detection, where the binary real/fake interface remains fixed while emerging attacks must be learned without forgetting previous ones. We introduce Fable-Bench, which organizes attack evolution through complementary joint-modality, text-side, and image-side protocols. We further propose ARISE (Authentic Reference-Informed Stability Enhancement), motivated by the open-ended forged class and the comparatively reusable geometry of authentic content. ARISE fits a real-only Gaussian mixture model to projected authentic replay representations as a compact historical reference. Meanwhile, the proposed Gaussian-Responsibility-Aware Stability Preservation (GRASP) derives a sample-adaptive anisotropic metric that strongly constrains historically stable representation directions while retaining plasticity elsewhere. Our Vulnerability-Aware Replay (VAR) further estimates stage-wise vulnerability from authentic-density degradation, forged-to-authentic boundary confusion, and authentic-mode occupancy drift, then assigns bounded replay emphasis to fragile stages. All adaptive signals are obtained from training-time replay statistics, while inference uses only the original multimodal backbone and binary classification head. Experiments across three attack-evolution protocols and multiple detector architectures demonstrate improved historical retention and final average performance over representative continual-learning baselines.
  </details>

- **[Diagnosing and Correcting Bias in MLLM for Long Video Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36210)**  `arXiv:2610.36210`  
  _Xusheng Liang, Jianqiao Sun, Hao Zhang, Yulei Niu, Hengshuang Zhao, Jiawei Ma_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Long-video question answering is challenging since the answer often hinges on a few decisive moments scattered throughout the video, while memory constraints force Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to sample frames at extremely low rates, resulting in sparsity that risks omitting key evidence. Though aggressively enlarging the context size is intuitive, we argue that performance remains fundamentally constrained by the bias, i.e., the misleading cues caused by spurious linguistic correlations and salient yet irrelevant visual observations. In this paper, we first introduce S-MME, a benchmark designed to systematically diagnose shortcut-biased behavior in MLLMs. To mitigate this failure, we further propose a training-free framework, Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning (CLEAR). By treating the full video-question pair as a complete view, CLEAR estimates bias effects via augmented views by only keeping the question or locally salient visual clips. Then, we intervene hidden states to mitigate the discrepancy at inference such that the correct answer can be predicted confidently. With experimental studies across five benchmarks, we show that our method is generalizable and can be integrated in different MLLMs, yielding consistent gains in prediction and robustness. We hope CLEAR can offer a complementary direction in test-time scaling for long-video understanding.
  </details>

- **[OVM-Occ: Open-Vocabulary Monocular Occupancy Prediction via Geometry-Aware Vision-Language Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35312)**  `arXiv:2610.35312`  
  _Shuyang Yu, Haibo Qin, Shaohan Hu, Wei Shan, Xiaoqing Guan, You Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Monocular occupancy prediction in indoor scenes aims to recover a scene's 3D geometry and semantics from a single RGB image. Existing methods are restricted to a closed set of predefined categories, limiting their ability to generalize to unseen categories. This limitation is particularly critical in indoor scenes, where objects exhibit highly diverse and fine-grained semantic categories. We study open-vocabulary monocular occupancy prediction for indoor scenes and present OVM-Occ, a Gaussian-based occupancy framework with an instance-aware vision-language teacher. Specifically, we adopt Language-Embedded Gaussians as the intermediate scene representation, propose a geometry-aware deformable attention module to refine Gaussian semantic features, and construct instance-level vision-language embeddings to provide reliable semantic supervision. We further introduce geometry-aware decoupled semantic distillation to mitigate the interference between geometry learning and semantic learning. To evaluate open-vocabulary occupancy prediction performance, we introduce OpenOcc-ScanNet and OpenOcc-Replica, two extended benchmarks with more diverse and fine-grained semantic categories. Experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in open-vocabulary monocular occupancy prediction for indoor scenes, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art approach by 12.2 mIoU and 0.6 IoU on the Occ-ScanNet dataset, with consistent gains under new open-vocabulary evaluation protocols.
  </details>

- **[Efficient Generative Image Compression with Quantized Latents Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29691)**  `arXiv:2610.29691`  
  _Hao Cao, Yinhuan Huang, Wenqi Guo, Yuan Shen, Jungong Han, Zhijin Qin_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Generative image compression (GIC) delivers strong perceptual quality. However, GIC methods with strong perceptual quality often rely on pretrained diffusion models with high latency, while recent lightweight GIC methods reduce latency but compromise perceptual quality. At low bitrates, coarse deterministic quantization can map nearby encoder latents representing different fine details to the same quantized point, making those details difficult to recover. Motivated by this, we propose GR-GIC which delivers competitive compression performance with fast inference. For better performance, we introduce Guided Refinement (GR), which combines latent refinement guided by entropy context with adaptive perturbations, jointly improving reconstruction at low bitrates. For fast inference, we introduce reorganized projected residual vector quantization, which equivalently reorganizes residual updates into low-dimensional lookups to expose greater parallelism and reduce latency. Experiments on Kodak show that GR-GIC achieves BD-rate savings of 22.09%, 42.14%, 19.35%, and 30.87% over OneDC for LPIPS, DISTS, PSNR, and FID, respectively. Moreover, our CUDA implementation encodes and decodes in 2.81 and 3.48 ms on an NVIDIA A100, achieving $27.36\times$ and $58.77\times$ speedups over the official OneDC implementation, respectively. We further evaluate GR-GIC on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, demonstrating competitive coding speed on edge hardware.
  </details>

- **[SemQAM: A Unified Generative Image Codec for Joint Semantic-Channel Coding and Modulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29643)**  `arXiv:2610.29643`  
  _Hao Cao, Jingkai Ying, Yinhuan Huang, Zhijin Qin, Yuan Shen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Conventional digital image transmission typically optimizes source coding, channel coding, and modulation separately, limiting how source representations adapt to channel impairments. Such impairments can corrupt the latent representations recovered at the receiver and propagate through autoregressive coding, degrading reconstruction quality. We propose SemQAM, a unified generative image codec that supports conventional source coding and joint semantic-channel coding and modulation within a single model. SemQAM represents latent features using vector quantization (VQ), maps the resulting indices to QAM symbols, and updates the codeword selected by the detected index, encouraging easily confused symbols to represent similar latent features. We also use the conditional expectation of received codewords to approximate the receiver reconstruction at the transmitter, reducing error propagation during autoregressive coding without feedback. In the special case of noiseless transmission, SemQAM reduces to a conventional source codec called SemQAM-C. Experiments show that (i) SemQAM-C achieves lower bitrates than OneDC at matched LPIPS and DISTS, with approximately $27\times$ faster decoding. (ii) Compared with the separated SemQAM-C system using LDPC and QAM, SemQAM further achieves BD-CBR savings of 30.85%, 28.06%, and 28.80% on LPIPS, DISTS, and FID, respectively, demonstrating the benefit of joint optimization.
  </details>

- **[MOSAIC: Learning Object-Centric Structural Representations for Remote Sensing Image Super-Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13547)**  `arXiv:2610.13547`  
  _Liuqian Wang, Hanyu Xie, Rongzhen Zhao, Qi Ming, Chunjie Ma, Wentao Chao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Remote sensing image super-resolution (RSISR) requires faithfully reconstructing small foreground objects, multi-scale structures, and repetitive spatial patterns from degraded observations. Despite recent advances in generative super-resolution, existing methods often rely on dense low-resolution (LR) conditioning, which can entangle salient foreground structures with dominant backgrounds and insufficiently exploit complementary structural evidence across scales and samples. To address these limitations, we propose MOSAIC, an object-centric structural representation learning framework that complements dense spatial conditioning with compact structural guidance for generative RSISR. Specifically, MOSAIC extracts object-centric structural slots to emphasize salient foreground evidence, adaptively integrates stable cross-scale structures with fine-grained details to address substantial scale variation, and exploits recurring spatial patterns through image-guided retrieval from a shared prototype memory. The resulting representations combine image-specific evidence with shared structural priors to provide scene-level guidance for faithful reconstruction. Extensive experiments on UCMerced, AID, and RSSCN7 demonstrate consistent PSNR improvements across $\times 2$ and $\times 4$ settings, with gains of 2.07, 4.54, and 1.49 dB over DiT4SR at $\times 4$, respectively, alongside favorable LPIPS results and improved structural preservation. The code will be publicly released.
  </details>

- **[DeepRFTv3: Deep Residual Fourier Convolution for Unified Image Deblurring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12941)**  `arXiv:2610.12941`  
  _Xintian Mao, Haofei Song, Huaiyuan Wang, Jiansheng Wang, Qingli Li, Yan Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Image deblurring is a fundamental task in computer vision, yet existing methods mainly specialize in isolated scenarios. Consequently, the deblurring performance of these models drops significantly across scenarios with different cameras and image contents. This motivates the development of a unified motion deblurring framework that can handle diverse blur patterns. To this end, we construct a multi-source dataset and develop a data pruning and quality control pipeline. Then, to restore blur images with various motion blur kernels across different scenarios, we propose a unified motion deblurring framework via Fourier Convolution Learning. Existing deblurring networks usually rely on pixel-level mappings and overlook the convolutional nature of blur. Thus, the network mostly fits the image content itself rather than learning the convolution process, making it difficult to handle multi-source blur images. Instead of relying on spatial mapping, we perform blur-adaptive global filter learning in Fourier space, which avoids the limited spatial support of kernel estimation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our unified model effectively handles motion blurs across diverse sources and scenes, achieving competitive performance across both in-domain and OOD benchmarks.
  </details>

- **[When Semantics Matter: Reliability-Aware Semantic-Rhythm Control for Co-Speech Gesture Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36685)**  `arXiv:2609.36685`  
  _Zhirui Xing, Ming Meng, Kaige Li, Ziyi Xu, Zhaoxin Fan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Co-speech gesture generation aims to synthesize natural gestures that are both temporally synchronized with speech and semantically consistent with the spoken content. Although recent methods can generate rhythmically plausible motions, they often rely heavily on acoustic prosody while underutilizing textual semantics, especially when semantic annotations are incomplete, noisy, or unavailable. Consequently, the generated gestures may follow speech rhythm while failing to express the intended semantics. To address this problem, we propose a reliability-aware semantic-rhythm control framework for co-speech gesture generation. We first learn a discrete motion prior that represents continuous gestures in a compact and structured motion-code space. We then introduce a dual-branch semantic contribution estimation mechanism consisting of a full multimodal branch and an audio-only branch. Their distributional discrepancy provides a model-based proxy for text-induced predictive influence, which is interpreted jointly with segment-level semantic relevance. Based on this estimate, a controllable semantic-rhythm objective selectively strengthens semantic guidance in content-relevant segments while limiting unnecessary semantic intervention in rhythm-dominant segments. Furthermore, we treat background noise as an acoustic reliability condition and introduce noise-conditioned feature modulation together with benefit-regularized latent perturbation to improve generation robustness under realistic acoustic environments. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a favorable balance among semantic expressiveness, rhythmic synchronization, motion diversity, and robustness, enabling reliable and controllable co-speech gesture generation.
  </details>

- **[SkillPE: Creativity-Oriented Cinematic Skill Evolution for Text-to-Video Prompt Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34335)**  `arXiv:2609.34335`  
  _Yanwei Huang, Mingxuan Zhu, Shujie Li, Shiyuan Liu, Yuanxing Zhang, Arpit Narechania_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Achieving high-quality cinematic text-to-video generation remains challenging for non-experts, whose prompts often lack professional narrative and creative design. Existing prompt enhancement (PE) methods and static cinematic skills offer limited capabilities for exploring diverse creative realizations. We propose SkillPE, a creativity-oriented PE framework that systematically evolves reusable cinematic skills through reference-guided exploration. Starting from expert-provided cinematic knowledge, SkillPE initializes and normalizes 20 structured seed skills. It then retrieves movie references categorized as resonators (good matches), dissonants (weak matches), and divergents (creatively inspiring near-misses). Resonators and dissonants refine skill applicability and execution, while divergents inspire alternative cinematic realizations through controlled mutations that preserve user intent.
